back.body: MEDICAL inverts TRAUMA · The story tells you more than your hands do · Scene safety + primary assessment FIRST regardless · RESPONSIVE: OPQRST + SAMPLE, then a focused exam aimed by the history · UNRESPONSIVE: rapid head-to-toe + vitals first, history from family, bottles, the room · Reassess 5 min unstable / 15 min stable
back.why_it_matters: The refrigerator full of insulin is history nobody asked for.

back.body: Chief complaint = what the PATIENT says, quoted · Never write your impression in that field · Common: chest pain, SOB, altered mental status, abdominal pain, weakness, dizziness, syncope, nausea/vomiting · VAGUE COMPLAINTS IN OLDER PATIENTS ARE HIGH RISK — cardiac events, sepsis and GI bleeds all present as 'just weak' · The complaint starts the questioning, it does not name the system

back.body: ISCHEMIC = blocked vessel = the large majority · HEMORRHAGIC = ruptured vessel = minority, more often sudden severe headache + vomiting + fast decline · YOU CANNOT TELL THEM APART IN THE FIELD and do not try · TIA = resolves completely = still a stroke warning = still transported · LAST KNOWN WELL is the history that matters — a time and a witness · AIRWAY BEFORE SCALE · CHECK A GLUCOSE ON EVERY ONE
back.why_it_matters: Last seen normal at ten at night, not found at seven in the morning. Nine hours decides what they can offer her.

back.body: CINCINNATI: facial droop · arm drift · speech · FAST = Face Arms Speech Time · BE-FAST adds BALANCE and EYES for posterior strokes · ONE abnormal finding = POSITIVE · A NEGATIVE SCALE DOES NOT RULE OUT A STROKE — believe the history · Last known well = time + witness · PRE-NOTIFY however close the hospital is
back.why_it_matters: FAST was negative three times on a woman having a posterior stroke.

back.body: B — Balance: sudden loss of balance or coordination · E — Eyes: sudden vision loss or double vision · F — Face: ask for a smile, watch for a lag · A — Arms: both out, eyes closed, watch for drift · S — Speech: repeat a sentence, listen for slurring · T — Time: last known well with a witness, and pre-notify

back.body: DURING: move furniture · pad the head · TIME IT · position for airway when you can · DO NOT RESTRAIN · PUT NOTHING IN THE MOUTH — the tongue cannot be swallowed · STATUS EPILEPTICUS = will not stop, or repeated without recovery = true emergency, expedite · POSTICTAL = confusion that GRADUALLY CLEARS; not clearing means look elsewhere · CHECK A GLUCOSE EVERY TIME
back.why_it_matters: Postictal patients get better. The one who is not getting better has something else going on.

front.title: Managing an active seizure
front.summary: Critical steps and the two nevers

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: protect from the environment, never restrain, never put anything in the mouth, time it, airway and suction when movement allows, oxygen and glucose, recognise status and expedite, reassess through the postictal period for steady improvement.
back.why_it_matters: The two nevers are reflexes people have to actively unlearn.

back.body: SYNCOPE = brief loss of consciousness from a dip in brain perfusion, FULL SPONTANEOUS RECOVERY · Quick and oriented = syncope; confused for a long time = postictal · VASOVAGAL usually has warning: light-headed, nausea, hot, vision greying · HIGH RISK: during EXERTION · NO warning at all · cardiac or family history of sudden death · A few jerks at the end can happen in a simple faint · THEY FELL — check the head
back.why_it_matters: He was up before anyone reached him, looking well, with three red flags in his history.

front.title: Headache red flags
front.summary: Most are not emergencies; find the ones that are

back.body: THE QUESTION: did it build up, or was it at its worst STRAIGHT AWAY? · 'Worst headache of my life' — believe it, especially from a frequent sufferer · FEVER + STIFF NECK = CNS infection, precautions · Any FOCAL DEFICIT, seizure or altered mental status · AFTER A HEAD INJURY, especially older or ANTICOAGULATED — mechanism need not look impressive · Wakes from sleep · worse on straining · new over 50 · CARE: dim, quiet, gentle, position of comfort, transport
back.why_it_matters: Her migraine history was exactly what made her able to say it was the worst she had ever had.

back.body: AMS ALWAYS HAS A CAUSE · Work AEIOU-TIPS rather than guessing · CHECK A GLUCOSE AND A SATURATION ON EVERY ALTERED PATIENT — the two reversible causes you can find · AVPU = the level; the differential = the cause; record BOTH · THE SMELL OF ALCOHOL EXCLUDES NOTHING — not low sugar, not a head injury, not sepsis · AIRWAY FIRST · Ask family what normal looks like
back.why_it_matters: He had been drinking all afternoon and his sugar was low. Both were true; one was going to kill him.

front.title: Insulin and glucose
front.summary: Fuel and the key to the door

back.body: GLUCOSE = the fuel · INSULIN = the key that lets it into cells · No key → glucose piles up in the blood WHILE THE CELLS STARVE · A HIGH READING DOES NOT MEAN FUELLED CELLS · The BRAIN fails first: no stores, no quick alternative → sugar problems look like brain problems · TYPE 1 makes none · TYPE 2 responds poorly and MAY STILL TAKE INSULIN · DOWN: medication without food, exertion, alcohol · UP: illness, infection, missed medication, stress
back.why_it_matters: A diabetic with flu usually runs high. The reflex expects low.

back.body: FAST onset: minutes to an hour · CONFUSED · odd or AGGRESSIVE · COOL PALE SWEATY · tremor · hungry · fast pulse → seizure → unresponsive · MIMICS drunkenness, psychiatric crisis and STROKE — which is why a meter comes out for EVERY altered patient · ORAL GLUCOSE ONLY IF THEY CAN SWALLOW AND PROTECT THEIR AIRWAY · Cannot protect it? NOTHING IN THE MOUTH — airway, transport, paramedic · Recheck after, and ask WHY it happened
back.why_it_matters: He was face down being handcuffed, soaked in sweat on a cold night, with a sugar of 2.1.

front.title: Hypo vs hyperglycemia
front.summary: Fast and sweaty, or slow and dry

back.body: See the comparison rows. The two shortcuts: ONSET — minutes versus days. SKIN — cool and sweaty versus warm and dry. Neither replaces a meter.
back.why_it_matters: Both end in an unresponsive diabetic. Only the meter tells you which one you are looking at.

back.body: SLOW onset: hours to DAYS · THE THREE POLYS: polyuria · polydipsia · polyphagia · PROFOUNDLY DEHYDRATED — glucose spills into urine and drags water with it · SKIN WARM DRY FLUSHED (mirror of hypo) · DKA: no usable glucose → burns FAT → ACID → DEEP SIGHING RESPIRATIONS blowing it off + SWEET/FRUITY BREATH · THAT BREATHING IS COMPENSATION — support it, never slow it · HHS: extreme glucose + profound dehydration, NO ketones, older type 2, slower still · CARE: airway, oxygen, position, TRANSPORT — fluid and insulin are not yours
back.why_it_matters: It looked like a respiratory call. The breathing was the only thing keeping his blood from turning to acid.

back.body: RARE — recognise, do not diagnose · OVERACTIVE THYROID: fever · very fast heart · agitated/confused · warm sweaty · UNDERACTIVE: cold · slow pulse · slow breathing · drowsy → unresponsive · ADRENAL CRISIS: weakness · vomiting · abdominal pain · SHOCK THAT DOES NOT RESPOND AS EXPECTED · THE KEY IS THE MEDICATION LIST: long-term steroids + unwell, injured, or recently stopped = adrenal crisis until proven otherwise · They need MORE steroid under stress, not less · CARE: supportive + temperature + transport
back.why_it_matters: They did not diagnose anything. They said the word steroid at handover, and that was enough.
